sections.h2: Which Anoka County office sends the property tax bill?
sections.html:
Property Records & Taxation does it all under one roof, from valuation to collection. The office is in the Government Center at 2100 3rd Avenue, Anoka, MN 55303. Phone 763-323-5400 for tax questions, or write to proptax@anokacountymn.gov about a valuation. Counter service runs weekdays from opening at eight in the morning until half past four, holidays excepted.

The county's Taxation page adds that Anoka County prints the proposed tax statements for a long list of taxing bodies at once: the county itself, your city, the school district and the state, depending on where the parcel sits and what type of property it is. The bill you pay is a combination of all of those levies.

sections.h2: What should a seller know about Anoka County itself?
sections.html:
Anoka County is bordered by Hennepin and Ramsey counties to the south. It has 446 square miles, with the Mississippi River along the southwestern boundary and the Rum River running south through the west. The terrain is low, rolling and wooded, and the lakes include Coon, Ham, Bunker and Centerville.

The county was organized by the Minnesota Territorial Legislature on May 23, 1857, out of parts of Ramsey and Benton counties. Its seat is the city of Anoka, a name from the Dakota word for "on both sides," a reference to the town's place on both banks of the Rum River. Twenty cities fall inside the county, among them Anoka, Blaine, Coon Rapids, Fridley, Columbia Heights, Andover, Ramsey, Lino Lakes and Ham Lake.

Census QuickFacts supplies these numbers:

  • 381,605 people in mid-2025, packed at 862.4 per square mile of land
  • 145,902 housing units, with 80.2% occupied by owners
  • Median value of an owned home of $346,500 (2020 to 2024)
  • Median gross rent of $1,464 and a typical owner payment of $1,949 with a mortgage
  • 774 building permits in 2025, and a household income median of $101,869

Twenty cities and one township fill the county, and the valuation appeal route depends on which city a house is in.

sections.h2: How does Anoka County value and classify a home?
sections.html:
The assessor values property as of January 2 each year and mails a Notice of Valuation and Classification. The estimated market value on that notice reflects what the assessor thinks the property would sell for on the open market. The class records how the property is used.

On a homestead, the notice also shows a Homestead Market Value Exclusion. The county's explanation gives the formula: a maximum of $38,000 at a market value of $95,000, falling by nine percent of the value above $95,000, and disappearing at $517,200. A seller whose house is worth more than that gets no exclusion, and a buyer in that range will see the full taxable value.

The notice lists other adjustments too, including an exclusion for veterans with disabilities, deferrals under Green Acres, Rural Preserve and Open Space, and a platted vacant land deferral. Taxable market value is the figure after all of those. A separate line shows new improvement value, the assessor's estimate of additions made in the past five years.

Higher value does not automatically raise your bill. The county notes that taxes follow the annual levy and how your value moves compared with neighboring properties.

sections.h2: How do I appeal an Anoka County valuation?
sections.html:
The path depends on your city, and the county's notice page spells it out. Your valuation notice tells you which option applies.

  • In a city that holds its own Local Board of Appeal and Equalization, you must appear there first if you want to go on to the county board.
  • In an Open Book city, you can skip straight to the County Board of Appeal and Equalization in June.
  • Either way, the County Board of Appeal and Equalization is the next stop if the first step did not settle things.

For a first conversation about the number itself, the Taxation page lists proptax@anokacountymn.gov and 763-323-5400. Have your parcel identification number ready.

Beyond the boards, Minnesota Statutes 278.01 lets an owner petition district court or the Tax Court by serving the county auditor, with proof of service filed by April 30 of the year the tax is payable. Statute 274.01 keeps local board meetings between April 1 and May 31.

sections.h2: How can I pay Anoka County property tax?
sections.html:
You can pay four ways, and the county sets out the costs for each. Taxes can be paid at PayAnokaCounty online, by mail, at the Government Center, or through a free automatic direct payment program.

Anoka County payment methods and what each costs (county Payment Options page)
MethodCostNotes
Online card, Apple Pay, Google Pay2.6% feeFee goes to the processor, not the county
Online eCheck$3.50Taken online only
Mail a checkNonePostmark must meet the due date; allow 2 weeks to post
In personNone for cash or check2.6% for cards; drop box available
Direct paymentFreePre-registration required; call 763-323-5400

The county warns that mail is sometimes not postmarked on the day it is dropped off. If the deadline is close, ask the post office counter for a hand-applied postmark, which is free. There is no grace period, and a due date that falls on a weekend rolls forward to Monday or the next business day. Payment due dates depend on how the property is classified.

sections.h2: When do Anoka County proposed tax statements arrive?
sections.html:
They are mailed in mid-November. The county calls them proposed 2027 property tax statements, and they are not final until the taxing bodies approve their levies in December. The county has posted budget and levy hearing dates on its Taxation page, and eNotices let an owner get the statement by email with the code printed on the proposed notice.

The county names four factors that move a bill: local levies from the city, school district and county, changes in the overall tax base, changes in your assessed value, and how your value change compares with others nearby. Hearings are for budgets, not valuations. The county says the Truth in Taxation meeting is not the place to argue your taxable market value.

The county also reports that in 2026 the legislature created a one-time increase of nearly 15% for homeowners who qualified for the 2025 regular property tax refund, with form M1PR due by August 15, 2027.

sections.h2: Who receives the Anoka County tax statement after I sell?
sections.html:
Often it is still you. Anoka County mails one statement per parcel a year, in mid-March, and a change in recorded ownership after January 1 does not trigger a new mailing. The statement goes to the previous owner or taxpayer, so a buyer and seller should plan for a duplicate request after closing.

A sale, a refinance or a mortgage satisfaction are the usual reasons for a different taxpayer, and each calls for a duplicate. Call 763-323-5400 if you have not received a statement by April 1. Not receiving one does not forgive the penalty or interest.

A manufactured home is taxed on a separate schedule, with statements mailed in July, and its title cannot be transferred until all current and delinquent personal property taxes are paid.

faqs.q: Where do I pay Anoka County property tax in person?
faqs.a: Go to the Government Center in Anoka at 2100 3rd Avenue on a weekday. A service counter and a payment drop box are available. Cash and checks carry no fee, while cards and mobile wallets add 2.6%.

faqs.q: Does Anoka County give a grace period on late taxes?
faqs.a: No. The county states plainly that there is none, and a payment made after either due date draws a penalty that grows the later you pay.

faqs.q: What is the Anoka County assessment date?
faqs.a: January 2 each year. The value notice reflects the assessor's view of what the property would sell for at that time, and the back of the notice lists your appeal options.

faqs.q: Can I appeal my Anoka County valuation at the county board without going to the city first?
faqs.a: Only if your city uses the Open Book format. Where a city holds its own Local Board of Appeal and Equalization, you must appear there before the June county board hearing.

faqs.q: Is the Anoka County proposed tax statement my final bill?
faqs.a: No. The proposed statement shows what you would pay in 2027 if the taxing bodies adopt the budgets they are considering. Levies are approved in December, and the final bill is mailed in mid-March.
